DEPARTMENT OPERATING SYSTEM

Custom Software & Enterprise Solutions Department Handbook

From zero to professional: business systems, engineering, client delivery, costing, templates and onboarding

Document VEL-CSE-001 · Version 1.0 (draft for management approval) · 4 November 2026 · Confidential — internal use

Engineer must verify

This handbook defines methods, controls and templates. It does not certify any system as secure, compliant or structurally/financially safe. Independent engineer or auditor review is required before production reliance. Vendor prices and tool versions must be re-verified from official sources on the day of use.

How to Use This Handbook

This handbook is the single operating manual of the Custom Software & Enterprise Solutions Department. It does two jobs: (1) it trains a beginner into a professional who can join supervised commercial software projects, and (2) it fixes the mandatory lifecycle, standards, templates, costing model and approval gates that every client project follows, from lead qualification to production support.

Golden rules
  1. Do not skip stages. A stage starts only when the previous stage's approval gate is signed.
  2. “It works on my laptop” is not “production-ready”. Production-ready means secure, tested, monitored, backed up, restorable, documented and handed over.
  3. Requirements are frozen in writing before design and development. Anything after the freeze is a change request.
  4. Never put passwords, keys or tokens in Git, chat, documents or tickets.
  5. Never run destructive commands (DROP, DELETE without WHERE, rm -rf) without understanding the effect and a verified backup.
  6. Never claim a system is “secure”, “compliant” or “guaranteed”. We offer readiness support; certification belongs to authorised auditors.
  7. Every production change has a second reviewer. Nobody approves their own work.
  8. Never design multi-tenancy unless the client has explicit tenant-isolation requirements — and then never ship it without isolation tests.

Reading path for a beginner

Part A · Foundations (Ch 1–3)→Part B · Technology & lifecycle (Ch 4–5)→Part C · Architecture & standards (Ch 6–7)→Part D · Business & people (Ch 8–9)→Part E · Projects & sources (Ch 10–11)→Appendices · Templates

How the module series works

The department curriculum is delivered one module at a time. This document is Module 0 — the Department Handbook and Onboarding Plan: it defines the whole system and gives each topic a summary pack. Each later module takes one level or lifecycle area and expands it into full lessons using the 14-point teaching structure in Chapter 2.

Currency of information

Tool versions, vendor prices and platform limits change. This handbook gives methods and formulas; every vendor price used in a quote must be re-verified on the vendor's official pricing page or calculator on the day of quoting and recorded with the date. Prices in worked examples are assumptions, not vendor quotes.

Sixteen commercially deliverable service lines. Each can be sold alone or combined into a multi-module programme.

Regulated domains

Hospital, school, payroll and financial systems hold sensitive personal data. We build the controls (access control, audit trails, encryption, consent capture) and say “compliance readiness support”. We never state a system is compliant or certified; the client's own legal/compliance owner signs that off.

Which service line first?

For a new department, sell in this order of delivery risk: billing/inventory/booking (small, clear scope) → CRM/HRMS/project (medium) → ERP/manufacturing/hospital (large, multi-module). Do not accept an ERP-scale programme until the team has delivered two medium projects and the Technical Lead has signed off the reference architecture.

2. Employee Teaching Standard

Every topic in every module is taught with the same 14-point structure. A topic is not complete until all fourteen points exist and the employee has been approved on it.

#PointWhat the lesson must contain
1What it isA plain-language definition in two sentences, with one real-world example.
2Why businesses need itThe business problem solved and the cost of not having it.
3How it worksA diagram or step list of the mechanism — not just the vocabulary.
4Tools requiredExact tools, versions policy and licence (free/permissive first).
5InstallationCopy-paste setup on the company standard workstation, with a check command.
6ImplementationA guided, working example built step by step.
7Expected resultWhat the finished output looks like (screen, output, file, test report).
8VerificationHow the employee proves it works: commands, tests, queries.
9Common errorsThe five most frequent mistakes with symptom → cause → fix.
10SecurityWhat can go wrong securely and the control that prevents it.
11DocumentationWhat must be written down (README, ADR, runbook, diagram) and where it is stored.
12Practical exerciseA task with no solution shown, scoped to 2–4 hours.
13AssessmentQuiz + demonstration with a pass mark (default ≥ 80 %).
14ApprovalNamed approver signs the topic in the employee's training record.
Pass rules

A level is passed only when every exercise is demonstrated live to the Technical Lead, every quiz is ≥ 80 %, and the level's capstone is reviewed. Re-sit allowed once per quiz after 3 working days of remedial study.

Worked example A — Database transactions (all 14 points)

PointLesson content
1. WhatA transaction is a group of database changes that either all succeed or all are undone (atomicity). Example: moving ₹1,000 from account A to B.
2. WhyWithout it, a crash between “debit A” and “credit B” loses money. ERP/billing data must always balance.
3. HowBEGIN → statements → COMMIT (make permanent) or ROLLBACK (undo). ACID: Atomic, Consistent, Isolated, Durable. Isolation levels control what concurrent users see.
4. ToolsPostgreSQL 16+ (or SQL Server / MySQL InnoDB), psql or Azure Data Studio/DBeaver, .NET 8 with EF Core or Npgsql.
5. Installdocker run --name pg -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=<local-dev-only> -p 5432:5432 -d postgres:16 → check: docker exec pg psql -U postgres -c "select version()".
6. ImplementSee SQL and C# below: create accounts, write a transfer, force a failure, observe rollback.
7. ResultAfter a forced failure, both balances are unchanged; after success, the total is unchanged.
8. VerifyRun select sum(balance) from accounts before/after: must be identical. Add an automated integration test.
9. ErrorsForgetting COMMIT (locks held); swallowing exceptions so rollback never happens; long transactions holding locks; mixing two connections in one logical unit; retrying non-idempotent work.
10. SecurityUse least-privilege DB accounts; parameterised queries only; never build SQL by string concatenation.
11. DocsRecord the unit-of-work boundary per use case in the architecture doc; note isolation level and retry policy.
12. ExerciseImplement “issue stock to production order” that decrements stock, inserts a movement row and writes an audit row atomically.
13. Assess10-question quiz + live demo of a rollback test.
14. ApproveTechnical Lead / Database Engineer signs “Transactions” in the training record.
sql
-- PostgreSQL
create table accounts(id int primary key, owner text not null, balance numeric(14,2) not null check (balance >= 0));
insert into accounts values (1,'A',5000),(2,'B',1000);

begin;
  update accounts set balance = balance - 1000 where id = 1;
  update accounts set balance = balance + 1000 where id = 2;
commit;           -- use ROLLBACK; to undo

select sum(balance) from accounts;   -- must stay 6000
csharp
// C# 12 / .NET 8 + EF Core — one business operation = one transaction
public async Task TransferAsync(int from, int to, decimal amount, CancellationToken ct)
{
    await using var tx = await _db.Database.BeginTransactionAsync(ct);
    try
    {
        var a = await _db.Accounts.SingleAsync(x => x.Id == from, ct);
        var b = await _db.Accounts.SingleAsync(x => x.Id == to, ct);
        if (a.Balance < amount) throw new DomainException("Insufficient balance");
        a.Balance -= amount; b.Balance += amount;
        _db.AuditLog.Add(AuditEntry.For("Transfer", from, to, amount));
        await _db.SaveChangesAsync(ct);
        await tx.CommitAsync(ct);
    }
    catch { await tx.RollbackAsync(ct); throw; }   // never swallow
}

Worked example B — Role-based access control (summary)

PointLesson content
What / WhyRBAC grants permissions to roles and roles to users. Businesses need it so clerks cannot approve payments and auditors can read but not edit.
HowAuthenticate (who) → load roles/claims → authorise each action (invoice.approve) on the server. UI hiding is cosmetic only.
ImplementASP.NET Core policies: [Authorize(Policy = "invoice.approve")]; permission table role_permission; deny by default.
VerifyA test per role × sensitive endpoint: allowed roles get 200, others 403; unauthenticated gets 401.
ErrorsChecking permission only in the frontend; role names hard-coded across code; forgetting object-level checks (user A reading user B's record — OWASP “Broken Access Control”).
SecurityDeny by default; log denials; review privileged roles quarterly; separation of duties (maker ≠ checker).
Convention

In Modules M1–M6 each topic appears as a full 14-point lesson file. In this handbook (M0) the roadmap in Chapter 3 gives the summary pack (definition → why → exercise → check) for every topic so that the whole system can be planned and approved first.

3. Training Roadmap: Levels 1–6

A beginner reaches supervised-project readiness in six levels (~ 90 days with the plan in Appendix B). Levels 1–2 are shared by everyone; from Level 3 the employee follows a role track (see Chapter 9).

L1 Business systems→L2 Business analysis→L3 Software engineering→L4 Database→L5 Enterprise architecture→L6 Professional engineering

Level 1 — Business Systems Fundamentals

Duration: 2 weeks · Tools: Excel/Sheets, draw.io, a notebook

TopicWhat it isWhy businesses need itExercise & check
How businesses operateOrganisations buy, make/serve, sell, collect cash and report.Software models these flows; if you don't understand them you build the wrong thing.Map how a local shop earns a rupee, from supplier to bank.
Departments & workflowsSales, purchase, stores, production, finance, HR, support — each with hand-offs.Most defects are hand-off gaps between departments.Draw the order-to-cash flow of a distributor.
Business processesA repeatable sequence of steps with inputs, outputs and an owner.Only a defined process can be automated or measured.Write one process as numbered steps with owner per step.
Users & rolesWho uses the system and what each is allowed to do.Drives permissions, screens and training.List 6 roles for a clinic and their allowed actions.
Records & transactionsA master record (customer) vs a transaction (invoice).Correct structure keeps reports and audits valid.Classify 15 fields as master / transaction / reference.
Approval workflowsA request moves through approvers by rules (amount, role).Controls spend and fraud; the most requested ERP feature.Design a 3-level purchase approval with limits.
ReportingTurning records into decisions: lists, summaries, dashboards.Clients buy software for the reports they get.Sketch 5 reports a store owner needs and their data fields.
Business rulesConditions the business enforces (credit limit, GST slab).Rules live in configuration/code and change often.Write 10 rules in “IF … THEN …” form.
Functional vs non-functional requirementsWhat the system does vs how well (speed, security, uptime).Non-functional gaps cause most production failures.Classify 20 sample requirements and add 5 missing NFRs.

Common mistakes: treating a spreadsheet column as a requirement; ignoring exceptions (returns, cancellations); mixing master and transaction data.

Capstone: Document one real small business (shop/clinic/tuition centre): departments, 3 workflows, roles, 5 reports.

Assessment: 30-question quiz ≥ 80 % + whiteboard the order-to-cash flow · Approval: Business Analyst lead

Level 2 — Business Analysis

Duration: 3 weeks · Tools: draw.io/BPMN, Excel, Markdown, Jira/GitHub Issues

TopicWhat it isWhy businesses need itExercise & check
Client discoveryStructured meetings to learn goals, pain and constraints.Wrong discovery = wrong product and disputed scope.Run a mock 45-min discovery; submit notes in the template.
Stakeholder interviewsQuestioning owners, users and IT using open, probing questions.Different stakeholders hold different truths.Interview a peer; list 3 conflicting statements.
Requirement gatheringCapturing, numbering and validating needs.Traceable IDs link need → design → test.Produce 25 numbered requirements (FR-001…).
Process mappingVisual flow with swimlanes, decisions and exceptions.Shows waste and automation points.Map a leave-approval process in BPMN.
AS-IS and TO-BECurrent process vs improved process after the system.Proves value; fixes scope boundary.Produce both diagrams and a gap list.
User stories“As a <role> I want <goal> so that <benefit>.”Small testable slices of value.Write 12 stories, each ≤ 3 days of work (INVEST).
Acceptance criteriaGiven/When/Then conditions that define “done”.Basis of UAT and payment milestones.3 criteria per story, all testable.
Use casesActor–system interaction with main and alternate flows.Covers exceptions developers miss.Write 3 use cases with 2 alternate flows each.
Scope managementIn-scope / out-of-scope / assumptions / dependencies.Prevents unpaid scope creep.Write the scope section of a SOW.
Change requestsFormal evaluation (impact on time/cost/risk) before changing scope.Protects margin and relationship.Price one change using the rate card (Ch 8).

Common mistakes: solution-first thinking (“we'll use a dashboard”) before problem definition; unmeasurable words (“fast”, “user-friendly”); no owner for each requirement.

Capstone: Full BRD + FRD (Appendix C/D templates) for a 4-module mini ERP with AS-IS/TO-BE maps.

Assessment: Requirement-review defence in front of a panel (scored on a rubric) · Approval: Business Analyst lead + Project Manager

Level 3 — Software Engineering

Duration: 4 weeks (track-based) · Tools: VS Code / Visual Studio, .NET 8 SDK or Python 3.12 + Node 20 LTS, Git, Postman/curl

TopicWhat it isWhy businesses need itExercise & check
Programming fundamentalsVariables, control flow, functions, collections, errors.Every later skill depends on it.Solve 20 graded problems (FizzBuzz → invoice totals).
C# & .NET 8 (or Python / TypeScript)Typed language and runtime used for most projects.Strong typing and tooling suit long-lived business systems.Build a console invoice calculator with unit tests.
Object-oriented programmingClasses, encapsulation, interfaces, inheritance vs composition.Models business entities and swaps implementations.Model Customer/Invoice/Payment with invariants.
APIsHTTP contracts (REST, JSON) between client and server.Web, mobile and integrations all use APIs.Design and call 5 endpoints; publish OpenAPI.
Backend architectureLayers: API → application → domain → infrastructure.Keeps rules testable and replaceable.Refactor a controller-heavy app into layers.
Frontend architectureComponents, state, routing, forms, API client.Users judge the product by the UI.Build a list/detail/edit screen in React + TypeScript.
AuthenticationProving identity (passwords, OIDC, MFA, JWT/cookies).Foundation of every control.Implement login with hashed passwords; no plain text.
AuthorisationDeciding what an identity may do (roles, policies, ownership).Prevents data exposure (OWASP A01).Add policy tests for 3 roles.
Error handlingConsistent, safe error responses and exceptions.Stable systems and safe messages.Return RFC 7807 problem details; no stack traces to clients.
LoggingStructured events with correlation IDs, no secrets.Support and audit depend on logs.Trace one request across logs using a correlation ID.

Common mistakes: business logic in controllers/UI; catching exceptions and ignoring them; logging passwords/tokens; trusting client-side validation.

Capstone: Employee-management API + web UI (Project P1 in Chapter 10).

Assessment: Code review pass (≥ 80 % rubric) + 60 % automated test coverage on domain code · Approval: Technical Lead

Level 4 — Database Engineering

Duration: 3 weeks · Tools: PostgreSQL 16+, SQL Server Developer/Express, MySQL 8, DBeaver/Azure Data Studio, Docker

TopicWhat it isWhy businesses need itExercise & check
Relational databasesTables, rows, keys and relationships.The core of almost every business system.Design 6 tables for a school with PK/FK.
SQLSELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, joins, grouping, window functions.Reports and troubleshooting need SQL fluency.Write 20 report queries from a sample schema.
PostgreSQLOpen-source RDBMS with rich types and strong standards support.Default choice for cost and portability.Install, create roles, restore a dump.
SQL ServerMicrosoft RDBMS, common in Windows/.NET shops.Many clients already own licences.Port a schema; compare identity vs sequences.
MySQLPopular open-source RDBMS (InnoDB).Common on shared hosting and PHP legacy.Note differences in quoting, AUTO_INCREMENT, defaults.
NormalisationRemoving duplication (1NF–3NF) so each fact is stored once.Prevents update anomalies and wrong totals.Normalise a denormalised invoice sheet to 3NF.
TransactionsACID units of work.Money and stock must never be half-updated.Rollback test (Chapter 2, Example A).
IndexesStructures that speed lookups at write/storage cost.Slow screens are usually missing indexes.Read an EXPLAIN plan; add and measure an index.
MigrationsVersioned, repeatable schema changes.Safe releases across dev/stage/prod.Add a column with EF Core/Flyway/Alembic; roll forward.
Data integrityPK, FK, UNIQUE, CHECK, NOT NULL, triggers sparingly.The database is the last line of defence.Break each constraint on purpose and show the error.
Backup & recoveryFull/differential/log backups; tested restores; RPO/RTO.A backup never restored is only a hope.Backup, drop a table, restore to a point in time.

Common mistakes: no foreign keys “for speed”; storing money as float; SELECT * in code; running migrations manually on production; never testing restores.

Capstone: Normalised schema + migrations + seed data + restore drill for the Inventory system (P2).

Assessment: SQL practical (timed) + restore drill witnessed by the Database Engineer · Approval: Database Engineer

Level 5 — Enterprise Architecture

Duration: 3 weeks · Tools: draw.io / C4 model, Docker Compose, RabbitMQ, Redis, OpenAPI

TopicWhat it isWhy businesses need itExercise & check
Modular monolithsOne deployable with strict internal module boundaries.Best default: simple to run, easy to split later.Split an app into 4 modules with enforced references.
Microservices & trade-offsIndependently deployed services with own data.Scale/teams benefits vs cost, latency, consistency pain.Write an ADR justifying monolith vs microservices for 3 cases.
Multi-tenancyOne system serving many customers with isolated data.SaaS economics — but a major leak risk.Only with explicit requirement: implement tenant filter + isolation tests.
Role-based accessRoles → permissions → users, plus data scope (branch/department).Segregation of duties.Permission matrix for 6 roles × 12 actions.
Audit trailsImmutable who/what/when/before/after records.Disputes, fraud checks, compliance support.Add audit on invoice edits; prove it cannot be altered by the app.
Workflow enginesConfigurable state machines for approvals.Business changes flows without redeploying.Model Draft→Submitted→Approved→Posted with guards.
NotificationsEmail/SMS/in-app/webhook events.Keeps users in the loop; reduces follow-ups.Outbox pattern: send reliably after commit.
ReportingOperational reports vs analytical (read replica, warehouse).Heavy reports must not slow transactions.Build 3 reports; show query plan and index.
Integration patternsREST, webhooks, queues, file exchange, idempotency, retries.Systems never live alone.Integrate a mock accounting API with retry + idempotency key.
Data migrationExtract → clean → map → load → reconcile.Go-live fails more from bad data than bad code.Migrate a messy CSV with a reconciliation report.

Common mistakes: microservices on day one; tenant ID forgotten on one query; audit written by the same code that can be bypassed; migrating without reconciliation totals.

Capstone: Architecture pack for the multi-module ERP prototype (P6).

Assessment: Architecture review board presentation (C4 L1–L3 + 3 ADRs) · Approval: Technical Lead + Enterprise Architect (external reviewer if none)

Duration: 3 weeks · Tools: Git, GitHub, GitHub Actions, Docker, a cloud sandbox with budget alert, OWASP ZAP/Dependency scanners

4. Technology Stack Evaluation

Technology is chosen from five factors: client environment, target platform, budget, employee skills and long-term maintainability. We never choose a tool because it is fashionable.

Evaluation of each option

TechnologyBest fitAvoid / cautionSkill & cost note
C# / .NET 8 + ASP.NET CoreLong-lived enterprise back-ends, Windows/Microsoft shops, strong typing, excellent tooling and performance.Teams with no .NET skills and tiny budgets.Free, open source; Visual Studio Community/VS Code. Default for backend.
WPFWindows-only desktop apps: billing counters, shop-floor stations, offline-capable tools.Anything needing browser/mobile access; Linux/macOS users.Runs only on Windows; use MVVM; keep logic in UI-free libraries.
React + TypeScriptRich web UIs, large ecosystem, hiring pool; portals and dashboards.Over-engineering simple CRUD; teams without TS discipline.Free. Default for web frontend.
AngularLarge teams wanting an opinionated, batteries-included framework.Small teams needing speed; steep learning curve.Free; choose when the client already runs Angular.
TypeScriptTyped JavaScript for front-end and Node tooling.Mixing any everywhere defeats its value.Mandatory for all JS code.
PythonData work, automation, integrations, AI features, quick prototypes.Very large strictly-typed domains without type-checking discipline.Free; use type hints + mypy/ruff.
FastAPIFast Python APIs with automatic OpenAPI and validation (Pydantic).Heavy admin-style apps better served by Django.Free; good for integration microservices.
PostgreSQLDefault OLTP database: standards-compliant, JSON, extensions, no licence fee.Clients locked to SQL Server tooling.Free; managed services are inexpensive.
SQL ServerClient already licensed; deep Microsoft integration; reporting tools.Licence cost for new, cost-sensitive clients.Licensing varies by edition — verify on Microsoft's site.
MySQLExisting LAMP/hosting estates; read-heavy simple workloads.Complex reporting/constraints vs PostgreSQL.Free community edition; know the storage-engine (InnoDB) behaviour.
RedisCaching, sessions, rate limiting, short-lived locks.Using it as the primary database for business records.Cache is disposable by design; never the system of record.
RabbitMQReliable background jobs, integration events, decoupling.Simple apps where a DB-backed job table suffices.Adds an operational component — justify in an ADR.
REST APIsDefault API style for web/mobile/integration; OpenAPI documented.Chatty fine-grained calls; use batching or GraphQL only if justified.Version URLs/headers; document in OpenAPI.
DockerReproducible packaging for dev, CI and deployment.Windows-GUI apps like WPF (not containerised).Free for small business per vendor terms — verify current licence terms.
GitHub ActionsCI/CD where code is on GitHub.Long, expensive builds without caching.Free quota varies by plan — verify on GitHub's pricing page.
AWS / Azure / GCPManaged hosting, databases, storage, identity, monitoring.Over-engineering (Kubernetes) for small apps.Choose by client's existing relationship, region/latency and your team's skills.

Weighted decision matrix (use in the architecture ADR)

Score each candidate 1–5 per factor, multiply by weight, sum. The weights below are the department default and may be changed only with written justification in the ADR.

OptionClient environment fit (25%)Target platform (20%)Budget (licence + hosting) (15%)Team skills available (20%)Long-term maintainability (20%)Weighted /5
A: .NET 8 + React + PostgreSQL455454.55
B: .NET 8 + WPF + SQL Server523443.70
C: FastAPI + React + PostgreSQL355343.90

Worked check for A: 4×0.25 + 5×0.20 + 5×0.15 + 4×0.20 + 5×0.20 = 1.00 + 1.00 + 0.75 + 0.80 + 1.00 = 4.55. The scores are illustrative for a typical web ERP; a Windows-only counter application would score B higher on platform fit.

Department default stacks

ScenarioDefault stackHosting default
Web ERP / CRM / HRMS / portalASP.NET Core 8 modular monolith · React + TypeScript · PostgreSQL · Redis (cache only)Managed PaaS container service + managed PostgreSQL
Microsoft-centric clientASP.NET Core 8 · Angular or React · SQL ServerAzure App Service + Azure SQL, or client's data centre
Windows counter/billing desktopWPF (MVVM) · UI-free domain libraries · SQL Server/PostgreSQL · optional sync APILocal/branch server + cloud backup
Integration & data automationPython 3.12 + FastAPI · RabbitMQ where needed · PostgreSQLContainer on the same platform
Legacy modernisationStrangler pattern: new .NET services/UI beside the old app, shared database first, then splitParallel run on staging
Rule: justify, don't presume

Microservices, Kubernetes, message brokers and multi-tenancy are not defaults. Each needs an Architecture Decision Record stating the requirement that forces it, the alternatives, and the cost of operating it.

5. Mandatory Client Project Lifecycle

Twenty-nine stages in five phases. For every stage this chapter states tasks, owners, inputs, outputs, templates, review requirements and the approval gate. No stage starts until the previous gate is signed.

A Discover & Define (1–12)→B Design & Plan (13–17)→C Build (18–21)→D Verify & Release (22–26)→E Adopt & Sustain (27–29)

Approval gates at a glance

GateAfter stageApprover(s)Evidence required
G1 Qualification1Department HeadScorecard ≥ 18/25
G2 Requirements freeze11Client sponsor, Department HeadSigned BRD/FRS/NFR/I-O/permission matrix
G3 Commercial approval12Department Head, clientSigned SOW, margin ≥ target, advance received
G4 Design approval13–15Technical Lead, client (UI)Architecture + ADRs, ERD, prototype signed
G5 Ready to build16–17Technical Lead, PMPlan, protected repo, CI skeleton
G6 Release candidate22QA Lead, Technical LeadNo open critical/high defects; coverage targets
G7 UAT sign-off23Client sponsorSigned UAT certificate
G8 Go-live25Department Head, clientRehearsal passed, backup verified, rollback plan
G9 Handover28Client, Department HeadHandover pack and certificate
Template codes

Appendices C–K of this handbook contain the full text of the core templates (BRD, FRD, SOW, DB, QA, UAT, deployment, handover, costing). Codes T01–T19 are template IDs reserved for the lighter working forms (scorecards, registers, minutes); they are produced in Modules M1–M6 and are not yet written — until then, use the checklist in the stage's Tasks row.

Phase A — Discover & Define (Stages 1–12)

Stage 01 — Lead qualification

OwnerA: Sales/Department Head · R: Business Analyst
Tasks• Capture lead source, contact, sector, problem statement, rough budget and timeline.
• Score fit: strategic fit, budget realism, decision-maker access, technical feasibility, risk (1–5 each).
• Reject or redirect unsuitable leads (illegal, no budget, impossible deadline, outside capability).
• Book a discovery meeting only for leads scoring ≥ 18/25.
InputsEnquiry, website form, referral note
OutputsLead scorecard, qualification note, Go/No-Go decision
TemplatesT01 Lead qualification form
ReviewDepartment Head reviews every lead scored 15–20
Approval gateG1 Qualification — Department Head signs Go/No-Go

Stage 02 — Client discovery

OwnerA: Project Manager · R: Business Analyst
Tasks• Prepare agenda and question bank; send pre-read.
• Run discovery workshop(s) with owner and department heads.
• Record goals, pains, current tools, volumes, locations, deadlines, constraints, budget bands.
• Send minutes within 24 h and get written acknowledgement.
InputsQualified lead, client documents (forms, reports, Excel sheets)
OutputsDiscovery notes, problem statement, success measures, initial risks
TemplatesT02 Discovery questionnaire & minutes
ReviewSecond BA reads notes for gaps
Approval gateClient acknowledges minutes by e-mail

Stage 03 — Business process study

OwnerA: Business Analyst · R: Business Analyst, Technical Lead (advice)
Tasks• Shadow users doing real work; collect real forms, spreadsheets, invoices, reports.
• List processes, triggers, steps, volumes, exceptions and pain points.
• Capture the business rules and calculations with worked examples from real data.
InputsDiscovery notes, sample documents
OutputsProcess inventory, business-rule catalogue, sample data set
TemplatesT03 Process inventory
ReviewPeer BA review
Approval gateClient department head confirms process inventory

Stage 04 — Stakeholder identification

OwnerA: Project Manager · R: Business Analyst
Tasks• Identify sponsor, decision-maker, process owners, end users, IT contact, finance approver, external parties.
• Build a power/interest map and communication plan; agree one single point of contact (SPOC) on each side.
• Agree decision rights: who can approve requirements, changes and UAT.
InputsOrg chart, discovery notes
OutputsStakeholder register, RACI for the project, communication plan
TemplatesT04 Stakeholder register
ReviewProject Manager review
Approval gateSponsor confirms decision-makers in writing

Stage 05 — AS-IS process documentation

OwnerA: Business Analyst · R: Business Analyst
Tasks• Draw each in-scope process end-to-end (BPMN swimlane) exactly as performed today.
• Annotate delays, duplicate entry, errors, controls and volumes.
• Validate with the people who do the work, not only managers.
InputsProcess inventory, shadowing notes
OutputsAS-IS process maps with pain points and metrics
TemplatesT05 BPMN/flow template
ReviewProcess owner walk-through; peer review
Approval gateProcess owners sign each AS-IS map as accurate

Stage 06 — TO-BE process design

OwnerA: Business Analyst · R: BA, Technical Lead
Tasks• Design the improved flow: remove duplication, add controls and approvals, define system vs manual steps.
• List automation points, new roles, and changes to current practice.
• Estimate the benefit (time saved, errors avoided) so the client sees value.
InputsApproved AS-IS maps
OutputsTO-BE maps, gap analysis, benefit estimate, change-impact list
TemplatesT05 BPMN/flow template, T06 Gap analysis
ReviewTechnical Lead checks feasibility; BA peer review
Approval gateSponsor approves TO-BE direction

Stage 07 — Functional requirement gathering

OwnerA: Business Analyst · R: Business Analyst
Tasks• Write numbered requirements (FR-001…) per module, each atomic, testable and traceable to a TO-BE step.
• Write user stories with Given/When/Then acceptance criteria and priority (MoSCoW).
• Record business rules, validations, calculations, reports and notifications.
InputsTO-BE maps, rule catalogue
OutputsFunctional Requirements Specification (FRS), user-story backlog, traceability matrix v0
TemplatesAppendix C/D (BRD & FRD)
ReviewBA peer + Technical Lead review for testability
Approval gateClient SPOC accepts FRS draft

Stage 08 — Non-functional requirements

OwnerA: Technical Lead · R: Technical Lead, BA
Tasks• Quantify performance (users, response time), availability, security, audit, retention, backup RPO/RTO, browser/device support, accessibility (WCAG 2.2 AA target), localisation.
• Record data volume growth and compliance-readiness needs.
• State every NFR with a number and a way to measure it.
InputsDiscovery notes, volumes
OutputsNFR specification with measurable targets
TemplatesT07 NFR catalogue
ReviewTechnical Lead + Security reviewer
Approval gateClient signs NFRs as part of freeze

Stage 09 — Input/output specification

OwnerA: Business Analyst · R: BA, Backend Developer
Tasks• List every screen input field (name, type, length, mandatory, validation, source).
• List every report/document/export/interface output (layout, filters, formulas, sample).
• Define import/export files and third-party interface contracts.
InputsFRS, sample documents
OutputsI/O specification, field dictionary, report catalogue, interface list
TemplatesT08 Field dictionary & report spec
ReviewDeveloper confirms feasibility; client confirms sample outputs
Approval gateClient signs sample outputs

Stage 10 — User roles & permissions

OwnerA: Technical Lead · R: BA, Backend Developer
Tasks• Define roles, permission matrix (role × action × data scope), separation of duties (maker ≠ checker), admin and support access rules.
• Define authentication method (SSO, e-mail+MFA) and session rules.
• Define audit events to record.
InputsFRS, stakeholder register
OutputsRole-permission matrix, audit-event list, auth approach
TemplatesT09 Permission matrix
ReviewSecurity review; client process owners
Approval gateClient approves matrix

Stage 11 — Requirements freeze

OwnerA: Project Manager · R: BA, Technical Lead
Tasks• Walk the client through FRS, NFR, I/O and permission matrix line by line.
• Resolve open issues; assign baseline version (e.g. FRS v1.0).
• Publish the change-request procedure; from here, changes follow Ch 8 pricing.
InputsAll Phase A documents
OutputsSigned baseline: BRD, FRS, NFR, I/O spec, permission matrix, traceability matrix
TemplatesT10 Requirements sign-off
ReviewDepartment Head + Technical Lead sign-off
Approval gateG2 Requirements freeze — client sponsor and Department Head sign

Stage 12 — SOW & commercial approval

OwnerA: Department Head · R: Project Manager, BA
Tasks• Convert baseline to modules, estimate with the costing model (Ch 8), add risk contingency.
• Draft SOW: scope, deliverables, milestones, acceptance, assumptions, exclusions, payments, warranty, support, IP, confidentiality, termination.
• Legal/finance review; negotiate; obtain signed SOW and advance payment.
InputsFrozen requirements, costing model
OutputsSigned SOW, quote, payment schedule, project charter
TemplatesAppendix E (SOW), costing spec
ReviewFinance (margin ≥ target), Legal, Technical Lead (estimate)
Approval gateG3 Commercial approval — Department Head signs; client signs SOW

Phase B — Design & Plan (Stages 13–17)

Stage 13 — Software architecture

OwnerA: Technical Lead · R: Technical Lead, Backend Developer
Tasks• Select style (default: modular monolith), modules and boundaries; apply the stack matrix (Ch 4).
• Draw C4 context/container/component diagrams.
• Write ADRs for each significant decision; define cross-cutting concerns (auth, logging, validation, error model, config, caching).
InputsFrozen requirements
OutputsArchitecture document, C4 diagrams, ADRs, tech-stack decision
TemplatesT11 Architecture & ADR templates
ReviewPeer architect/Technical Lead from another project + Security
Approval gateG4 Design approval (with stages 14–15)

Stage 14 — Database architecture

OwnerA: Database Engineer · R: Database Engineer
Tasks• Model entities (ERD) in 3NF; define keys, constraints, indexes, naming, audit columns and soft-delete policy.
• Plan migrations, seed/reference data, partitioning/archival, backup and restore strategy with RPO/RTO.
• Where multi-tenant is required: choose isolation model and write tenant-isolation tests first.
InputsFRS, field dictionary, NFRs
OutputsERD, data dictionary, DDL draft, migration plan, backup plan
TemplatesAppendix F (DB checklist)
ReviewSecond Database Engineer/Technical Lead
Approval gateIncluded in G4

Stage 15 — UI/UX design

OwnerA: Frontend Developer (UX lead) · R: Frontend Developer, BA
Tasks• Create navigation map and wireframes per role; apply design system and accessibility rules.
• Prototype key flows (clickable); usability-test with 3 real users.
• Define empty/error/loading states and print layouts.
InputsFRS, I/O spec, brand guide
OutputsWireframes, clickable prototype, UI standards, accessibility notes
TemplatesT12 Wireframe & UI checklist
ReviewBA validates against stories; client approves prototype
Approval gateIncluded in G4 — client signs prototype

Stage 16 — Development planning

OwnerA: Project Manager · R: Technical Lead, PM
Tasks• Break work into epics → stories → tasks; estimate in ideal days with a 3-point range; order by risk and value.
• Plan 2-week sprints, definition of ready/done, environments, risks, resource plan and release schedule.
• Agree reporting rhythm: weekly status, fortnightly demo.
InputsArchitecture, backlog
OutputsRelease plan, sprint-1 backlog, RAID log, resource plan
TemplatesT13 Project plan & RAID log
ReviewTechnical Lead and Department Head
Approval gateG5 Ready to build

Stage 17 — Repository creation

OwnerA: Technical Lead · R: Technical Lead
Tasks• Create the repository from the department template (Ch 6); protect main; enable required reviews and status checks.
• Configure secret scanning, dependency alerts, CODEOWNERS, issue/PR templates, labels.
• Add CI skeleton (build + test + lint) and local dev docker compose environment.
InputsArchitecture, standards
OutputsRepository, CI skeleton, branch rules, developer README
TemplatesRepo template, PR template
ReviewAnother engineer clones and runs it in < 30 min
Approval gateIncluded in G5

Phase C — Build (Stages 18–21)

Stage 18 — Module-wise development

OwnerA: Technical Lead · R: Developers (Backend/Frontend/Junior)
Tasks• Develop module by module in vertical slices; each story ends with tests, docs and a demo.
• Follow standards (Ch 7): layers, validation, transactions, audit, RBAC, error model.
• Every PR: small, linked to story, reviewed by someone else, CI green before merge.
InputsSprint backlog, architecture, UI prototype
OutputsWorking, tested increments each sprint; updated docs; release notes
TemplatesT14 PR checklist, Definition of Done
ReviewMandatory PR review; Technical Lead reviews architecture-affecting PRs
Approval gateSprint review accepted by Product Owner (client SPOC)

Stage 19 — API & integration development

OwnerA: Technical Lead · R: Integration Engineer
Tasks• Design APIs contract-first (OpenAPI); version them.
• Build adapters for accounting, payment, SMS/e-mail, biometric, government portals; use idempotency keys, retries with back-off, timeouts, dead-letter queues.
• Stub third parties in tests; log every call with correlation ID, never secrets.
InputsInterface list, vendor API docs
OutputsAPI specs, adapters, integration test suite, runbook for failures
TemplatesT15 Integration design sheet
ReviewTechnical Lead; vendor sandbox test evidence
Approval gateIntegration test pass report

Stage 20 — Database migration (schema)

OwnerA: Database Engineer · R: Database Engineer, Backend Developer
Tasks• Write forward-only versioned migrations; test on a production-sized copy; measure lock time.
• Use expand → migrate → contract for breaking changes; never edit an applied migration.
• Script seeds for reference data; rehearse rollback/restore.
InputsDDL draft, ERD
OutputsMigration scripts, seed data, rehearsal log
TemplatesAppendix F (DB checklist)
ReviewDatabase Engineer peer
Approval gateMigration rehearsal signed by Technical Lead

Stage 21 — Security implementation

OwnerA: Technical Lead · R: All developers; Security reviewer
Tasks• Implement authN/authZ, input validation, output encoding, secure file upload, secrets management, TLS, rate limiting, audit logging.
• Run SAST, dependency, secret and container scans in CI; fix criticals before release.
• Threat-model each module (STRIDE) and test against the OWASP ASVS/Top 10 checklist.
InputsPermission matrix, NFRs, threat model
OutputsSecurity test report, scan results, hardening checklist
TemplatesT16 Security checklist
ReviewIndependent reviewer (not the author)
Approval gateNo open critical/high findings without written risk acceptance

Phase D — Verify & Release (Stages 22–26)

Stage 22 — Testing

OwnerA: QA Engineer · R: QA, Developers
Tasks• Execute unit, integration, system, regression, performance, security and accessibility tests; trace each FR to ≥ 1 test.
• Log defects with severity, steps, evidence; retest fixes; maintain regression pack.
• Report coverage, defect density and open defects daily in the final week.
InputsBuild, FRS, test plan
OutputsTest plan, cases, execution reports, defect log, release-candidate report
TemplatesAppendix H (QA checklist)
ReviewQA Lead sign-off; Technical Lead review
Approval gateG6 Release candidate — zero open critical/high defects

Stage 23 — User acceptance testing (UAT)

OwnerA: Project Manager · R: Client SPOC, BA, QA
Tasks• Prepare UAT scripts from acceptance criteria with real sample data; train UAT testers.
• Client executes scripts in staging; defects triaged within 24 h; retest.
• Record formal acceptance, per module.
InputsRelease candidate on staging, UAT scripts
OutputsUAT results, sign-off certificate, accepted-defect list
TemplatesAppendix I (UAT checklist)
ReviewBA verifies each criterion; PM manages issues
Approval gateG7 UAT sign-off — client sponsor signs

Stage 24 — Staging deployment

OwnerA: Technical Lead · R: Backend Developer, DevOps support
Tasks• Deploy with the same pipeline and configuration shape as production; use masked/synthetic data.
• Run smoke tests, performance baseline and restore drill; rehearse the production runbook.
• Freeze the release candidate (tag, SBOM, image digest).
InputsRelease candidate, runbook
OutputsStaging environment, rehearsal log, release notes
TemplatesAppendix J (Deployment checklist)
ReviewSecond engineer executes the runbook from the document only
Approval gateRehearsal passed

Stage 25 — Production deployment

OwnerA: Technical Lead · R: Backend Developer, Support Engineer
Tasks• Announce change window; take verified backup; deploy via pipeline; run smoke tests; monitor 24–72 h hyper-care.
• Execute rollback if exit criteria fail.
• Record change, approver, time, result.
InputsSigned UAT, rehearsed runbook, backup
OutputsLive system, release record, monitoring in place, hyper-care log
TemplatesAppendix J (Deployment checklist)
ReviewChange approver ≠ deployer
Approval gateG8 Go-live — Department Head + client sponsor approve

Stage 26 — Data migration (go-live load)

OwnerA: Database Engineer · R: DB Engineer, BA, Client data owner
Tasks• Extract from legacy; cleanse and map; load in rehearsals (≥ 2 dry runs); reconcile counts, totals and samples.
• Client data owner signs reconciliation before cut-over; keep a read-only legacy copy.
• Run final delta load in the cut-over window.
InputsMapping sheets, legacy extracts
OutputsMigrated data, reconciliation report, exception list
TemplatesT17 Data-migration plan & reconciliation
ReviewClient data owner + DB Engineer sign
Approval gateReconciliation signed (record counts and financial totals match)

Phase E — Adopt & Sustain (Stages 27–29)

Stage 27 — Employee (end-user) training

OwnerA: Project Manager · R: BA, Support Engineer
Tasks• Create role-based training plan, user manuals, quick guides, short videos and FAQs.
• Train admins and users in small groups on staging with realistic data; test with a short quiz.
• Appoint super-users inside the client.
InputsFinal UI, manuals
OutputsTraining materials, attendance, assessment results, super-user list
TemplatesT18 Training plan & attendance
ReviewClient HR/department head confirms attendance
Approval gate≥ 90 % of users trained before go-live

Stage 28 — Client handover

OwnerA: Project Manager · R: Technical Lead, Support Engineer
Tasks• Hand over source/IP per SOW, credentials via secure vault, architecture, runbooks, backup/restore guide, API docs, user manuals.
• Walk the client IT through operations; transfer ownership of accounts and domains.
• Close the project: lessons learned, final invoice, satisfaction survey.
InputsAll deliverables
OutputsHandover pack, signed acceptance, support contact matrix
TemplatesAppendix K (Handover checklist)
ReviewTechnical Lead and Department Head
Approval gateG9 Handover — client signs handover certificate

Stage 29 — Maintenance & upgrades

OwnerA: Support Lead · R: Support Engineer, Developers
Tasks• Operate the support desk with SLA tiers (P1–P4), monitoring, monthly patching, backup verification and monthly report.
• Triage requests: bug (warranty) / change request (priced) / enhancement (roadmap).
• Plan upgrades: runtime/framework, database, dependencies and annual architecture health check; propose roadmap.
InputsSupport contract, monitoring, backlog
OutputsMonthly report, patched system, upgrade roadmap, renewal proposal
TemplatesT19 SLA & monthly report
ReviewTechnical Lead quarterly review
Approval gateClient approves each upgrade window

6. Enterprise Project Folder Structure

Every client repository starts from the same template so any engineer can find anything in seconds. The structure follows Clean/Onion layering (domain at the centre, infrastructure at the edge) inside a modular monolith by default.

tree
enterprise-software-project/
├── README.md                    # what it is, how to run in <30 min, links to docs
├── CONTRIBUTING.md              # branching, commits, PR rules, Definition of Done
├── CODEOWNERS                   # mandatory reviewers per path
├── docs/
│   ├── business-requirements/   # BRD, stakeholder register, AS-IS / TO-BE maps
│   ├── functional-requirements/ # FRS, user stories, field dictionary, traceability
│   ├── workflows/               # BPMN / state diagrams, approval matrices
│   ├── architecture/            # C4 diagrams, ADRs (adr-0001-*.md), NFRs
│   ├── database/                # ERD, data dictionary, migration & backup plan
│   ├── api/                     # OpenAPI files, integration contracts
│   └── user-manuals/            # role-based guides, training material, FAQ
├── src/
│   ├── frontend/                # React/Angular app (or WPF shell)
│   ├── backend/                 # API host: controllers/endpoints, DI, middleware
│   ├── domain/                  # entities, value objects, domain rules (no I/O)
│   ├── application/             # use cases, commands/queries, validators, interfaces
│   ├── infrastructure/          # EF Core/SQL repositories, e-mail, storage, clock
│   └── integrations/            # adapters to accounting, payment, SMS, government APIs
├── database/
│   ├── migrations/              # versioned, forward-only scripts
│   ├── seeds/                   # reference data (roles, tax codes, statuses)
│   └── scripts/                 # backup, restore, reporting views, maintenance
├── tests/
│   ├── unit/                    # fast tests: domain + application
│   ├── integration/             # real DB (container) + API tests
│   ├── system/                  # end-to-end, performance, security checks
│   └── acceptance/              # UAT scripts mapped to acceptance criteria
├── deployment/                  # Dockerfiles, compose, IaC, runbooks, release notes
├── security/                    # threat models, security checklist, scan config, policies
├── monitoring/                  # dashboards, alert rules, health-check definitions, SLOs
└── .github/
    └── workflows/               # ci.yml, security.yml, deploy-staging.yml, deploy-prod.yml

What each directory is for

DirectoryPurposeRules
docs/business-requirementsThe why: BRD, stakeholders, AS-IS/TO-BE.Signed versions are immutable; changes create a new version.
docs/functional-requirementsThe what: FRS, stories, field dictionary, traceability matrix.Every FR ID appears in at least one test.
docs/workflowsApproval flows and state machines.Diagrams stored as source (.bpmn, .drawio) plus exported PNG.
docs/architectureC4 diagrams, ADRs, NFRs.One ADR per significant decision; never delete, supersede.
docs/databaseERD, data dictionary, backup/restore plan.Updated in the same PR as any migration.
docs/apiOpenAPI specs and integration contracts.Generated or validated in CI; breaking changes need version bump.
docs/user-manualsEnd-user and admin guides.Written for roles, with screenshots from staging.
src/domainEntities, value objects, domain services and rules.No references to database, HTTP or UI frameworks.
src/applicationUse cases, DTOs, validators, ports (interfaces).Defines transactions boundaries; depends only on domain.
src/infrastructureImplementations of ports: EF Core, storage, e-mail, clock.Replaceable; contains no business rules.
src/backendComposition root: endpoints, auth, DI, logging, health checks.Thin — maps HTTP to use cases.
src/integrationsAnti-corruption adapters to external systems.One folder per external system; contract tests with recorded samples.
src/frontendUI application.Talks to the backend only through the generated API client.
database/migrationsVersioned schema changes (V0001__create_party.sql).Applied migrations are never edited.
database/seedsReference data only; no personal data.Idempotent scripts.
database/scriptsBackup/restore/maintenance scripts.Dry-run flag and confirmation prompt on destructive scripts.
tests/*Test pyramid layers.Unit tests run < 2 minutes; integration tests use disposable containers.
deploymentDockerfiles, compose, IaC, runbooks.No secrets; configuration via environment/secret store.
securityThreat models, checklist, scan configs, risk register.Reviewed every release.
monitoringDashboards-as-code, alert rules, SLOs.Every alert has an owner and a runbook link.
.github/workflowsCI/CD pipelines.Pinned action versions; least-privilege tokens.

Adapting the structure to the chosen architecture

ArchitectureAdaptation
Modular monolith (default)Inside src/, give each business module its own folder per layer or its own project: src/modules/inventory/{domain,application,infrastructure}. Modules talk through public interfaces or in-process events only; an architecture test fails the build on forbidden references.
Microservices (justified by ADR)One repository per service or a mono-repo with services/<name>/ each having its own src/, database/, deployment/. Add contracts/ (OpenAPI/AsyncAPI) and platform/ (gateway, broker, observability). Each service owns its database — no shared tables.
WPF desktopsrc/frontend becomes src/desktop-wpf (MVVM). Keep domain/application UI-free class libraries so the same rules can serve a future web API. deployment/ holds the installer (MSIX/WiX) and update channel.
React + FastAPIsrc/backend is the Python package (app/api, app/services, app/models, alembic/); domain/application/infrastructure map to app/domain, app/services, app/repositories.
Legacy modernisationAdd legacy/ (read-only snapshots, schema dumps) and docs/migration/ (mapping sheets, reconciliation reports, strangler routing table).
Definition of a ready repository (Stage 17)

A new engineer can clone, run docker compose up, run the tests and open the app in under 30 minutes using only the README.

7. Mandatory Enterprise Engineering Standards

These sixteen standards are enforced in code review and CI. Each has a rule, an implementation pattern and a verification. A standard may be waived only by the Technical Lead, in writing, with a risk note in the ADR log.

#StandardRuleHow we verify
1Modular architectureBusiness capabilities are modules with explicit public APIs.Architecture tests block forbidden dependencies.
2Separation of concernsUI, API, application, domain and persistence are separate layers; no business logic in controllers or SQL triggers.Code review checklist; layering tests.
3Reusable business componentsShared concerns (numbering series, tax, approval, attachments, audit) are built once in a shared kernel.No duplicate logic in PR review.
4Database integrityPK/FK/UNIQUE/CHECK/NOT NULL on every table; money as numeric/decimal; UTC timestamps.DB checklist (Appendix F).
5Transaction managementOne use case = one transaction; explicit boundaries; optimistic concurrency on editable records.Rollback and concurrency tests.
6Role-based access controlDeny by default; permission checks server-side at endpoint and object level.Permission-matrix test per role.
7Audit logsWho/what/when/old/new for every create/update/delete/approve; append-only.Audit tests; DB account cannot update/delete audit rows.
8Multi-tenant isolationOnly if the client requires it. Tenant ID on every row, enforced centrally (global filter + DB row-level security where available).Mandatory cross-tenant tests (below).
9Data validationValidate at the edge (shape/type/range) and in the domain (business rules) and in the DB (constraints).Negative tests for each rule.
10Secure file handlingWhitelist type by content, size limit, random storage names, outside web root, malware scan hook, signed download links.Upload abuse tests.
11Backup & restoreAutomated backups, off-site copy, encrypted, restore drill each quarter; RPO/RTO documented.Drill report.
12API securityTLS only; authN on every endpoint; rate limits; input limits; CORS allow-list; no sensitive data in URLs; OWASP API Top 10 review.ZAP/automated scan + manual checklist.
13PerformanceBudgets in NFRs (e.g. p95 < 500 ms for list screens); pagination everywhere; indexes justified by query plans; no N+1.Load test + query-plan review.
14AccessibilityWCAG 2.2 AA target: keyboard operable, labels, contrast, focus order, error text.axe/Lighthouse + manual keyboard test.
15VersioningSemantic versioning for releases; API versions; DB migration versions; documented deprecations.Release checklist.
16DocumentationREADME, ADRs, API docs, runbooks, user manuals updated in the same PR as the change.PR template checkbox; docs build in CI.

Implementation patterns

Transaction + audit in one unit of work (standards 5 and 7)

csharp
public sealed class ApproveInvoiceHandler(AppDbContext db, ICurrentUser user, IClock clock)
{
    public async Task Handle(Guid invoiceId, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        await using var tx = await db.Database.BeginTransactionAsync(ct);
        var inv = await db.Invoices.SingleAsync(i => i.Id == invoiceId, ct);      // tenant filter applied globally
        if (inv.CreatedBy == user.Id) throw new DomainException("Maker cannot approve own invoice.");
        var before = inv.Status;
        inv.Approve(user.Id, clock.UtcNow);                                       // domain rule inside entity
        db.Audit.Add(new AuditEntry("Invoice", inv.Id, "Approve", before, inv.Status, user.Id, clock.UtcNow));
        await db.SaveChangesAsync(ct);                                            // RowVersion concurrency token checked
        await tx.CommitAsync(ct);
    }
}

Multi-tenant isolation (standard 8) — only with explicit requirement

Never design multi-tenancy without explicit tenant-isolation requirements and tests

Before any tenant column is added, the SOW/FRS must state: how many tenants, isolation level (shared schema / schema-per-tenant / database-per-tenant), who may see cross-tenant data (nobody by default), and what happens on tenant offboarding. If these are missing, stop and ask — build single-tenant.

csharp / sql
// EF Core global query filter — every tenant-owned entity implements ITenantOwned
modelBuilder.Entity<Invoice>().HasQueryFilter(e => e.TenantId == _tenant.Id);

// PostgreSQL defence in depth (row-level security)
alter table invoice enable row level security;
create policy tenant_isolation on invoice
  using (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::uuid);
csharp
// Mandatory isolation tests (xUnit) — a build with any failing test cannot be released
[Fact] public async Task TenantA_cannot_read_TenantB_invoice() { /* seed B, query as A -> empty/404 */ }
[Fact] public async Task TenantA_cannot_update_TenantB_invoice_by_guessing_id() { /* expect 404/403, row unchanged */ }
[Fact] public async Task Reports_and_exports_filter_by_tenant() { }
[Fact] public async Task Background_jobs_run_with_explicit_tenant_context() { }
[Fact] public async Task Missing_tenant_context_fails_closed() { /* no tenant -> exception, not 'all rows' */ }

Secure file upload (standard 10)

csharp
var allowed = new Dictionary<string, byte[]> { [".pdf"] = "%PDF"u8.ToArray(), [".png"] = [0x89,0x50,0x4E,0x47] };
if (file.Length is 0 or > 10_000_000) return Results.BadRequest("Invalid size");
var ext = Path.GetExtension(file.FileName).ToLowerInvariant();
if (!allowed.TryGetValue(ext, out var magic)) return Results.BadRequest("Type not allowed");
await using var s = file.OpenReadStream(); var head = new byte[magic.Length]; await s.ReadExactlyAsync(head);
if (!head.SequenceEqual(magic)) return Results.BadRequest("Content mismatch");
var stored = $"{Guid.NewGuid():N}{ext}";             // never trust the client file name
await storage.SaveAsync(stored, s, ct);               // outside web root; scan hook; DB keeps metadata

Validation at three levels (standard 9)

LevelExampleWhy
Edge (API)Required, length ≤ 100, valid e-mail, amount > 0Fail fast with 400 and field-level messages.
DomainCredit limit not exceeded; cannot ship more than orderedRules hold no matter which client calls.
DatabaseCHECK (qty >= 0), UNIQUE (tenant_id, invoice_no)Last line of defence against bugs and direct SQL.
Structural/regulatory honesty

Standards reduce risk; they do not guarantee security or legal compliance. Security reports carry the line “Independent engineer/auditor review required before production reliance.”

8. Costing and Commercial Model

Price = cost to deliver ÷ (1 − target gross margin), built bottom-up from effort, never from what the client “can afford”. All figures below are worked illustrations with internal assumptions (INR, ex-GST); recalibrate rates from timesheets each quarter.

Vendor pricing — verify before quoting

Hosting, database, licence and SaaS prices change. The hosting and licence lines below are allowances, not vendor quotes. Before any quotation, price the real services in the official calculators — AWS Pricing Calculator, Azure Pricing Calculator, Google Cloud Pricing Calculator, GitHub Plans & pricing, Microsoft SQL Server pricing — and record the date, region, SKU and screenshot in the quote file. GST/tax treatment must be confirmed with the finance owner and official tax portal.

Cost components (all 17 must appear in every estimate)

Formulas
  1. Labour cost = Σ (days × cost/day). Contingency = labour × risk % (small 10 %, medium 15 %, enterprise 20 %).
  2. Direct cost = labour + contingency + licences + build-period hosting. Price = direct cost ÷ (1 − 40%).
  3. Gross margin % = (price − direct cost) ÷ price. Discounts reduce margin 1:1 — never discount without Department Head approval.
  4. Break-even projects per year = 12 × monthly non-billable overhead ÷ gross margin per project.
  5. Annual support = support % × project price; annual hosting = monthly hosting × 12 × 1.15 (management fee).

Commercial rules

TopicPolicy
Payment schedule (default)30 % on SOW signature · 30 % on design approval (G4) · 30 % on UAT sign-off (G7) · 10 % on go-live + 30 days (G8/G9). Adjust only with Department Head approval.
Estimate validity30 days; re-verify vendor prices at signature.
WarrantyDefects against signed requirements fixed free for 60–90 days after go-live; enhancements are change requests.
Discount authority≤ 5 %: Project Manager · ≤ 10 %: Department Head · > 10 %: Director. Margin floor 30 %.
Fixed price vs T&MFixed price only after requirements freeze; T&M for discovery, legacy investigation and unclear scope.
Hosting/licencesClient-owned accounts preferred; if resold, show pass-through and management fee separately.
TaxesQuotes are ex-tax; apply GST/other taxes per current law as confirmed by Finance.

Change-request pricing

  1. Log the CR (ID, requester, description, reason, priority). The client SPOC must request in writing.
  2. BA performs impact assessment (scope, schedule, cost, risk, tests, docs) — charged at 0.5 day BA rate as a minimum fee, credited if the CR is approved.
  3. Price = Σ(role days × rate card) + 20 % premium if raised after requirements freeze (G2), 0 % if it replaces an equal-size in-scope item (scope swap).
  4. Client approves in writing; Project Manager updates SOW schedule and baseline; only then is work started.

Worked example (Medium project): “Add a stock-transfer approval step between warehouses” — BA 1 d, Dev 4 d, QA 2 d, DB 0.5 d.

LineAmount
Impact assessment (0.5 d BA at rate card)₹3,333
Work: 1×BA + 4×Dev + 2×QA + 0.5×DB at rate card₹50,833
Post-freeze premium (20 % of work)₹10,167
Change-request price (ex-tax)₹64,333
Fixing the numbers

These examples exist to teach the method. Do not quote a client from this chapter: build the real estimate with the Costing Model Specification (Appendix L), get Technical Lead review of the days, and Finance review of margin.

9. Employee Roles, Responsibility Matrix and Approvals

Ten roles, each with defined responsibilities, entry level and approval authority. In a startup one person may hold several roles, but the author of work is never its approver.

RolePrimary responsibilityMinimum level to work unsupervisedKey outputs
Business AnalystDiscovery, requirements, process maps, UAT preparation, change impact.Levels 1–2 + Level 3 basicsBRD, FRS, stories, UAT scripts
Junior Software DeveloperImplements assigned stories under review; writes tests.Level 3 · pairs with a seniorPRs, unit tests
Backend DeveloperAPIs, domain logic, security, transactions, performance.Levels 3, 4(basic), 6Services, API docs, tests
Frontend DeveloperUI, accessibility, UX prototypes, API client.Level 3 (frontend track), 6UI components, prototypes
Database EngineerERD, migrations, performance, backup/restore, data migration.Levels 4–5ERD, migrations, restore drills
Integration EngineerThird-party and legacy interfaces, queues, idempotency.Levels 3, 5Adapters, contract tests
QA EngineerTest strategy, automation, defect management, UAT support.Levels 1–2, 3 basics, 6Test plan, reports
Technical LeadArchitecture, standards, estimates, code/PR gatekeeping, mentoring.All levels + 3 delivered projectsADRs, reviews, approvals
Project ManagerScope, plan, risks, budget, communication, gates, change control.Levels 1–2 + PM trainingPlans, status reports, change log
Support EngineerMonitoring, tickets, patching, backups verification, monthly reports.Levels 4 basics, 6Tickets, reports, runbooks

Responsibility matrix (RACI)

R = does the work · A = accountable (one per row; signs) · C = consulted · I = informed. Roles: BA, JD (Junior Dev), BD (Backend), FD (Frontend), DB, IE (Integration), QA, TL (Technical Lead), PM, SE (Support). The Department Head additionally signs gates G1, G3, G8 and G9 and is accountable above the matrix.

Segregation of duties

The developer of a change cannot approve its PR; the person who deploys cannot be the sole approver of the change; the person who prepares a quote cannot approve it; production credentials are never shared.

10. Practical Training Projects and Sign-off

Seven projects, completed in order, each in the employee's personal sandbox with a budget alert. Each is reviewed by the Technical Lead against its acceptance criteria. Evidence (repo link, test report, screenshots, handover pack) goes in the portfolio. Projects 1–6 are individual; Project 7 is a team simulation.

P1 — Employee Management System

GoalMaster data, departments, documents and basic HR workflows; the first full-stack CRUD with RBAC.
Key requirements• Employee master (personal, job, contact), departments, designations, reporting manager.
• Roles: HR Admin (full), Manager (own team, read), Employee (own profile, read).
• Document upload (ID proof) with secure file handling; audit log of edits.
• Search/filter/pagination; export to CSV (HR Admin only).
Database designdepartment, designation, employee (FK dept, desig, manager_id self-FK), employee_document, app_user, role, user_role, audit_log. Unique employee_code; CHECK (date_of_joining <= current_date).
Code deliverablesASP.NET Core 8 API (layers per Ch 6), EF Core migrations, React + TypeScript screens (list/detail/edit), JWT/cookie auth, OpenAPI.
Testing≥ 60 % unit coverage on domain/application; integration tests with a PostgreSQL container; role × endpoint permission tests; upload abuse tests.
Handover packREADME (run in < 30 min), ERD, API docs, 1-page admin guide, seed script.
Acceptance criteriaAll tests green in CI; manager cannot read another team; audit row exists for each update; uploaded .exe renamed .pdf is rejected.
sql
create table employee (
  id              uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
  employee_code   varchar(20)  not null unique,
  full_name       varchar(150) not null,
  email           varchar(254) not null unique,
  department_id   int          not null references department(id),
  designation_id  int          not null references designation(id),
  manager_id      uuid         references employee(id),
  date_of_joining date         not null check (date_of_joining <= current_date),
  status          varchar(12)  not null default 'Active' check (status in ('Active','Inactive','Exited')),
  row_version     bigint       not null default 0,
  created_at      timestamptz  not null default now()
);
create index ix_employee_department on employee(department_id);
create index ix_employee_manager on employee(manager_id);

P2 — Inventory Management System

GoalStock accuracy through movements: the ledger is truth, balances are derived.
Key requirements• Items (SKU, UoM, reorder level), warehouses, suppliers.
• Goods receipt, issue, transfer, adjustment — each creates immutable movement rows.
• Stock on hand per warehouse, low-stock report, stock valuation (weighted average).
• Negative stock blocked unless permission granted and audited.
Database designitem, warehouse, supplier, stock_movement(id, item_id, warehouse_id, qty_signed, unit_cost, ref_type, ref_id, created_at), grn, grn_line, issue. Balance = Σ qty_signed (view/materialised table updated in the same transaction).
Code deliverablesDomain service StockService (pure, deterministic), application commands, API, simple UI. Golden tests below.
TestingHand-calculated tests: receive 10 @ ₹100, receive 10 @ ₹120 → average ₹110; issue 5 → 15 units × ₹110 = ₹1,650. Concurrency test: two simultaneous issues cannot overdraw.
Handover packERD, stock-valuation rule note, restore drill record, user guide.
Acceptance criteriaΣ movements = reported balance for all items; transfer is atomic (both rows or none); concurrency test passes; restore drill witnessed.
csharp
[Fact] // Weighted average — hand calculation: (10*100 + 10*120)/20 = 110; after issue 5 -> 15 units, value 1650
public void Weighted_average_cost_after_two_receipts_and_one_issue()
{
    var s = new StockLedger();
    s.Receive(qty: 10, unitCost: 100m); s.Receive(qty: 10, unitCost: 120m);
    s.AverageCost.Should().Be(110m);
    s.Issue(5);
    s.OnHand.Should().Be(15); s.Value.Should().Be(1650m);
}

P3 — CRM Prototype

GoalCapture and progress leads to won/lost deals with a visible pipeline.
Key requirements• Lead capture (web form + manual), owner assignment, duplicate detection by phone/e-mail.
• Pipeline stages with configurable probabilities; activities (call, meeting, task); follow-up reminders.
• Convert lead → account + contact + opportunity; reports: conversion rate, pipeline value, activity by owner.
Database designlead, account, contact, opportunity(stage_id, amount numeric(14,2), expected_close), pipeline_stage, activity, note, user_owner. Unique partial index on normalised phone.
Code deliverablesREST API, Kanban board UI (React), background reminder job (outbox pattern).
TestingStory-level acceptance tests (Given/When/Then); duplicate-detection test; forecast calculation golden test: weighted pipeline = Σ amount × probability.
Handover packBA pack (AS-IS/TO-BE, stories), ERD, demo script, user guide.
Acceptance criteriaSales user sees only own leads; manager sees team; forecast numbers match hand calculation on seed data.

P4 — Billing Application

GoalAccurate, auditable invoicing with tax and payments.
Key requirements• Customers, items/services, tax rates (from reference table / rule pack — never hard-coded).
• Quote → invoice → payment → receipt; credit notes; numbering series per financial year without gaps.
• Invoice PDF, payment allocation, outstanding ageing report, reminders.
Database designcustomer, item, tax_rate, invoice, invoice_line, payment, payment_allocation, credit_note, number_series. Money numeric(14,2); line total stored; invoice immutable after posting.
Code deliverablesDomain InvoiceCalculator (rounding policy documented), posting use case in one transaction with audit and number allocation.
TestingGolden test: 2 × ₹500 = ₹1,000 + 18 % tax ₹180 = ₹1,180. Rounding tests (half-up per line vs per invoice as stated in SOW). Gap-free numbering test under concurrency.
Handover packTax configuration guide, ERD, sample invoices, runbook for number-series repair (never manual SQL).
Acceptance criteriaTotals match hand calculations; posted invoice cannot be edited (only credited); ageing report reconciles to ledger.
csharp
[Fact] // 2 x 500 = 1000; tax 18% = 180; total = 1180   (rate comes from tax_rate table, not code)
public void Invoice_total_with_single_tax_rate()
{
    var inv = Invoice.Draft(customerId);
    inv.AddLine(itemId, qty: 2, unitPrice: 500m, taxRate: 0.18m);
    inv.SubTotal.Should().Be(1000m); inv.TaxTotal.Should().Be(180m); inv.GrandTotal.Should().Be(1180m);
}

P5 — Role-based Enterprise Portal

GoalA portal for customers/vendors/employees with fine-grained access, notifications and audit.
Key requirements• Login with MFA option; roles and permissions managed by admin; data scope (own company/branch).
• Self-service: view orders/invoices, raise tickets, upload documents, download statements.
• Notifications (e-mail/in-app) via outbox; full audit trail; admin activity report.
Database designapp_user, role, permission, role_permission, user_scope, ticket, notification_outbox, audit_log. Row-level scope applied by a central query filter.
Code deliverablesPermission policies, scope filter, outbox dispatcher, admin UI. If tenant isolation is required: tenant filter + RLS (Ch 7) — otherwise not built.
TestingPermission-matrix test (role × endpoint); IDOR tests (user A requests user B's record id); session-expiry and lock-out tests; accessibility check (axe + keyboard).
Handover packThreat model (STRIDE table), permission matrix, security checklist, user and admin guides.
Acceptance criteriaEvery IDOR attempt returns 404/403 and is logged; no endpoint without authorisation attribute; ZAP baseline scan has no high findings.

P6 — Multi-module ERP Prototype

GoalIntegrate Masters, Sales, Purchase, Inventory, Finance-lite and HR-lite as a modular monolith.
Key requirements• Module boundaries with public interfaces; shared kernel (numbering, approval, attachments, audit).
• Order-to-cash and procure-to-pay flows end-to-end; approval workflow with limits.
• Posting to a simple ledger (double entry: debits = credits); dashboard and 5 reports.
Database designPer-module schemas (sales.*, inventory.*, finance.*), ledger_entry (debit, credit, account), approval_request, approval_step. Cross-module references by ID only.
Code deliverablesArchitecture tests forbidding cross-module references; domain events (in-process) with outbox; CI pipeline to staging.
TestingEnd-to-end scenario tests: sales order → stock issue → invoice → payment → ledger balances; trial balance debits = credits; performance baseline.
Handover packC4 diagrams, 3+ ADRs, module catalogue, runbook, release notes.
Acceptance criteriaTrial balance balances after the scenario suite; architecture tests pass; fresh clone runs in < 30 min.

P7 — Complete Simulated Client Project

GoalA supervised team (BA, 2 developers, QA, PM) runs all 29 lifecycle stages for a fictional client (e.g. a 40-bed clinic or a 5-branch distributor).
Key requirements• Role-play client provided by the Technical Lead with realistic messy data and a change request injected in week 4.
• All templates (Appendices C–L) completed; all gates G1–G9 executed with sign-offs.
• Costing and SOW prepared by the team; margin reviewed by Department Head.
Database designDesigned by the team (3NF ERD, migrations, seed + migrated legacy CSV with reconciliation).
Code deliverablesDeployed to staging and a production-like environment with CI/CD, monitoring and backups.
TestingFull test plan, UAT executed by the role-play client, security checklist, restore drill, performance baseline.
Handover packComplete handover pack (Appendix K), training session delivered, lessons-learned report.
Acceptance criteriaDepartment Head's panel marks each gate evidence; any missing gate evidence = fail until fixed.
Sign-off statement

“I have reviewed the evidence for this project against its acceptance criteria. The employee has demonstrated the skills listed and may work on supervised client projects at this level.” — Technical Lead (name, date, signature). Sign-off is supervised-practice readiness, not independence or certification.

Appendix F — Database Design Checklist

Modelling

  • Entities and relationships trace to FR IDs.
  • 3NF unless a documented, measured reason to denormalise.
  • Naming convention applied (snake_case, singular tables, _id keys).
  • Master vs transaction vs reference tables separated.

Integrity

  • Every table has a primary key.
  • Foreign keys exist for every relationship (with defined ON DELETE behaviour).
  • UNIQUE constraints for natural keys (e.g. invoice number per period).
  • CHECK constraints for ranges/statuses; NOT NULL by default.
  • Money in numeric/decimal(14,2), never float; timestamps in UTC (timestamptz/datetime2).

Concurrency & transactions

  • Transaction boundary per use case documented.
  • Row-version/optimistic concurrency on editable records.
  • Gap-free number series use a locked counter row, not MAX()+1.

Performance

  • Indexes on FKs and common filters; each justified by a query plan.
  • No SELECT * in application code; pagination on all list queries.
  • Reporting queries tested with production-scale data.

Security

  • Least-privilege DB accounts (app ≠ migration ≠ admin).
  • Sensitive columns identified; encryption at rest/in transit; masking in non-production.
  • Audit table append-only (no UPDATE/DELETE grants).
  • If multi-tenant is explicitly required: tenant_id + isolation tests.

Migrations

  • Forward-only versioned scripts; applied scripts never edited.
  • Rehearsed on production-sized copy; lock duration measured.
  • Rollback = restore or compensating migration documented.

Backup & recovery

  • Backup schedule and retention documented; off-site encrypted copy.
  • RPO/RTO agreed with client.
  • Restore tested and recorded (date, duration, result).

Documentation

  • ERD current; data dictionary lists each column's meaning, type and source.

Approval

RoleNameSignatureDate
Database Engineer
Technical Lead

Appendix G — Code Review and Security Checklist

Pull-request review

  • Linked to a story/defect; scope is small and focused.
  • Tests added/updated and meaningful; CI green.
  • No business logic in controllers/UI; layering respected.
  • Validation at edge, domain and DB where relevant.
  • Errors handled; no swallowed exceptions; safe messages to clients.
  • Logging has correlation ID and no secrets/PII.
  • Docs/ADR/OpenAPI updated.
  • Migrations reviewed by Database Engineer.

Security (OWASP Top 10 aligned)

  • Access control: server-side checks at endpoint and object level (A01).
  • Cryptography: TLS everywhere; passwords hashed with a modern adaptive algorithm (Argon2id/bcrypt/PBKDF2); keys in a secret store (A02).
  • Injection: parameterised queries; encoded output (A03).
  • Insecure design: threat model and abuse cases exist (A04).
  • Misconfiguration: debug off, headers set, default accounts removed, CORS allow-list (A05).
  • Vulnerable components: dependency/SBOM scan and update plan (A06).
  • AuthN failures: MFA option, lock-out, session expiry, no credential stuffing paths (A07).
  • Integrity: signed builds/pinned actions; no unsafe deserialisation (A08).
  • Logging & monitoring: security events logged and alerted (A09).
  • SSRF: outbound allow-list for URL fetchers (A10).
  • Secret scan passes; no secrets in repo history.
  • File upload rules (Ch 7) applied.

Approval

RoleNameSignatureDate
Reviewer
Technical Lead

Appendix H — QA Checklist

Test planning

  • Test plan approved: scope, levels, environments, data, tools, entry/exit criteria, risks.
  • Every FR and NFR traced to ≥ 1 test case (traceability matrix).
  • Defect severity scale agreed (Critical/High/Medium/Low) with fix targets.

Execution

  • Unit tests pass; coverage target met on domain/application code (default ≥ 70 %).
  • Integration tests pass against a real database container.
  • System tests cover each end-to-end business scenario incl. exception paths (cancel, reverse, reject).
  • Regression suite executed on the release candidate.
  • Boundary, negative and invalid-input tests for every form and API.
  • Permission tests: every role × sensitive action; unauthenticated access rejected.
  • If multi-tenant: cross-tenant read/write/report/job tests pass.
  • Concurrency tests: double-submit, simultaneous edits, number-series.
  • Calculations verified against hand-calculated golden values from the client's real examples.
  • Data-integrity: totals, counts and ledger balances reconcile after test scenarios.
  • Performance test meets NFRs (p95, concurrency, report duration).
  • Security scan (SAST/dependencies/secrets/container) clean of critical/high.
  • Accessibility: keyboard-only walk-through; axe/Lighthouse results recorded.
  • Cross-browser/device matrix tested as per NFR.
  • Backup restore tested; log/alert samples verified.
  • Print/PDF/export outputs match approved samples.

Exit criteria for Release Candidate (G6)

Appendix I — User Acceptance Testing (UAT) Checklist

Preparation

  • Release candidate deployed to staging with production-like configuration and realistic (masked) data.
  • UAT scripts derived from acceptance criteria; each has steps, test data and expected result.
  • UAT testers named by the client (one per role) and trained for 1–2 hours; UAT window agreed.
  • Defect logging channel and triage rhythm (daily, within 24 h) agreed.
  • Entry criterion: G6 passed.

Execution

  • Each script executed by a real user, not by the project team.
  • Results recorded: Pass / Fail / Blocked with evidence (screenshot, record ID).
  • Defects triaged: defect (fix now) vs change request (price) vs training issue.
  • Fixes retested by the original tester; regression by QA.
  • Business reports and printed documents checked against approved samples.
  • Role permissions verified by the process owners.
